title: Haiti rice tariff cut
point: Artibonite Valley, Haiti's main rice-growing area (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Haiti cut rice tariffs in 1995 under an IMF structural adjustment programme (Oxfam). The IMF and the US set a general tariff cut as a condition for President Aristide's return in 1994/95.

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Foreign Policy describes the program as run by the IMF and World Bank; Oxfam says both kept pushing for low tariffs.

conditions: Rice import tariff cut in one step in 1995 as part of a structural adjustment program. Oxfam (2002): from 35% to 3%. Foreign Policy (2013): from 50% to 3%. Haiti's bound WTO tariff stayed at 50%.
community: Rice imports, mostly subsidized US rice, rose thirty-fold from 1985 to 1999. Local output fell from over 110,000 tonnes (1985) to about 80,000 tonnes (1995). Oxfam counted about 52,000 rice farmers, 85% on under 1 hectare; Foreign Policy cites about 130,000 in the Artibonite. Haiti now gets over 80% of its rice from the US. Farmers call the policy the 'death plan'.
outcome: In 2010 Bill Clinton told the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee: 'It may have been good for some of my farmers in Arkansas, but it has not worked. It was a mistake.' He added that he lives with 'the consequences of the lost capacity to produce a rice crop in Haiti'.

sources.title: Rice Dumping in Haiti and the Development Box Proposal
Bill Clinton's trade policies destroyed Haitian rice farming

confidence_note: Sources disagree on the starting tariff (35% Oxfam, 50% Foreign Policy) and on the number of rice farmers (52,000 vs 130,000). Clinton's apology was about US rice subsidies and policy, not the IMF.
